scenes.name: Lite metal: pop metal y glam
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: El subgénero que, desde 1983-84, intensifica el polo melódico del heavy y lo mezcla con el hard rock, quitándole el grave grueso. Philip Bashe lo llamó «metal pop» y señaló a Def Leppard y Van Halen; otros ejemplos son Poison, Bon Jovi, Ratt y Cinderella. Sus detractores, el público tradicional y el del thrash, lo llaman «poseurs», «false metal», «nerf metal», «poodle bands» o «glam», motes que describen bien sus rasgos: falta de autenticidad, pelo cardado, ropa colorida en lugar del negro obrero. Voz dulce sin gruñidos, armonías al modo de Aerosmith y Kiss, letras de amor y lujuria con nombres de chica y, sobre todo, la power ballad, que entra en radios que excluían el heavy y gana público nuevo, como las versiones blancas de Pat Boone en los cincuenta. MTV impulsó mucho su desarrollo. Se queda con la herencia dionisíaca y elimina el caos: «lo realmente pesado se quita».

podcast.title: Station Nightclub Fire (February 20, 2003)
podcast.body: On February 20, 2003, during a Great White performance at the Station Nightclub in Warwick, Rhode Island, pyrotechnics ignited flammable acoustic foam on the walls and ceilings. Within approximately one minute, the club was engulfed in flames, and within two minutes, visibility was lost due to thick black smoke. The subsequent rush to escape led to 100 deaths and 230 injuries. "Great white was performing when some pyro ignited some flammable acoustic foam in the walls and ceilings, like this."

podcast.title: The Station Nightclub Fire (2003)
podcast.body: The band was tragically involved in the Station Nightclub fire in February 2003 in West Warwick, Rhode Island. The incident resulted in 100 fatalities, including the band's guitar player, when pyro at the start of their set ignited insulation, causing the venue to go up in flames. "He was the singer of the band Great White, the group that was involved in the horrible station nightclub fire in February 2003, where 100 people, including Great White's guitar player, died. Some pyro went very wrong at the start of Great White's set, and some insulation went up in flames."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Station Nightclub Fire (February 20, 2003)
podcast.body: On February 20, 2003, during a Great White concert at The Station Nightclub in West Warwick, Rhode Island (mistakenly referred to as Long Island in the transcript), a pyrotechnic display at the start of their set ignited flammable foam insulation on the club's walls and ceiling. The entire building was engulfed in flames within six minutes, resulting in 230 injuries and 100 deaths, including Great White guitarist Ty Longley and a local radio DJ who was MCing the event. The tragedy led to criminal trials, civil lawsuits totaling approximately $176 million in settlements, and the imprisonment of one of the club's owners. Crucially, the disaster prompted significant increases in insurance requirements and the implementation of new, stringent safety protocols for indoor shows worldwide, making venues generally safer after this date. "Something went terribly wrong with the pyro display that started their set."

podcast.title: Ty Longley's Death
podcast.body: Ty Longley, guitarist for Great White, was among the 100 fatalities in The Station Nightclub fire on February 20, 2003. He died when a pyrotechnic display during the band's set ignited flammable foam insulation, causing the club to burn down in just six minutes. "100 died, including Great White guitarist Ty Longley and a local radio DJ who was MCing the show."

concerts.body: The location in West Warwick, Rhode Island (referred to as Long Island in the transcript), where Great White was booked to play a 450-capacity club on February 20, 2003, leading to a catastrophic fire during their performance.
